# Estimates of temporary employment

In this exercise, we will recreate an ONS labour market estimate published online in the table [EMP07 Temporary Employees](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/employmentandemployeetypes/datasets/temporaryemployeesemp07). Currently, this table is updated four times a year in February, May, August and November using the Quarterly Labour Force Survey (QLFS).

Learning outcomes:

-   To become more familiar with quarterly LFS datasets.
-   To become familiar with weighted population counts and their confidence interval
-   To understand how some ONS estimates are produced

## Data

The data used in this exercise relates to an estimate published by the ONS for October-December 2024.

To follow the exercise, you need to access the relevant dataset from the UK Data Service: [SN 9349: Quarterly Labour Force Survey, October - December, 2024](https://beta.ukdataservice.ac.uk/datacatalogue/studies/study?id=9349).

## Get set-up

We suggest that you create a folder named `LFS_exercises` as the working directory for this exercise -- where syntax files and other materials will be stored. After downloading the data, save it in an easily accessible location within `LFS_exercises`, such as a subfolder named `Data`.

First let's load the packages that we are going to need.

```{r prep}
library(haven)  ### Functions to open Stata or SPSS datasets
library(dplyr)  ### Easier data manipulation 
library(survey) ### Survey data analysis functions
library(srvyr)  ### Easier  manipulation of survey data
```

Set the working directory using `setwd ("LFS_exercises").`

And open the QLFS dataset.

```{r open}
setwd ("~")

# Import  the data from a Stata format dataset 
lfs_od24 <- read_dta(
              "Data/lfs/UKDA-9349-stata/stata/stata13/lfsp_od24_eul_pwt24.dta"
              )
```

Inspect the dataset and find out the number of cases and variables.

```{r dim}
ncol(lfs_od24) # Number of columns
nrow(lfs_od24) # Number of rows (observations)
```

## Questions

1.  What does the variable `INECAC05` record? 

2.  Why are there many missing cases on the variables: `JBTP101`, `FTPT` and `JOBTYP`?

## Answers

1.  `INECAC05` records `{r} labelled::var_label(dataex1$INECAC05)`

2.  Most of the missing cases are due to the variables not being applicable to all respondents. For example, the variable `FTPT` applies only to individuals aged 16 and over who are in employment. Similarly, `JBPT01`only applies to respondents who indicated that their job was not permanent in some way (i.e. where *JOBTYP = 2*).
:::

## Getting weighted frequencies

To get correct estimates of population values, we need to use the weighting variable - `PWT24`.

We will use `as_survey_design()`, an R function from the `survey` and `srvyr` packages, to create a weighted version of our data.

Let's first examine the variable `JOBTYP`, which indicates whether respondents work in a temporary job or not. 

```{r freqs}
t<-table(
  Freq=as_factor(
    dataex1$JOBTYP
    )
  )

t
```

Since we have missing values (e.g. 'Does not apply'), we can mark them as system missing (NA in R) in order to get neater tables.

```{r jobtmp}
 
dataex1 <- dataex1 |> 
          mutate (JobTmp =case_when(
                  JOBTYP== 1 ~ "Not temporary",
                  JOBTYP == 2 ~ "Temporary",
                  JOBTYP == -9  | JOBTYP == -8 ~ NA),
                  JobTmp = as.factor(JobTmp)
          )


tm<-table(Freq=dataex1$JobTmp)
tm
```

Let's create a version of the data with the weights applied, which we will use in the rest of the analysis.

```{r svydes}
dataex1.s<-dataex1|> 
         as_survey_design(weights=PWT24)
```

<!-- Note: In the code above, we removed observations with missing weight values. These cases should not be taken into account when calculating population estimates – and if we don't remove them, R will return an error message. -->

... And  compute the weighted frequencies of `JobTmp`.

We will look at the population counts first:

```{r svyfreqs}

### Simple point estimates
t1<-svytable(~JobTmp, dataex1.s)

cbind(Unweighted=tm,Weighted=t1)

```

... Then their 95% confidence interval:

```{r tci}
tci<-dataex1.s  |>
  filter(JobTmp=="Temporary") |>
  summarise(
    Temps = survey_total(vartype = "ci",na.rm=T)
  )

tci

### Another way of obtaining the same results

tci<-dataex1.s  |>
  filter(JOBTYP==2) |>
  summarise(
    total = survey_total(vartype = "ci",na.rm=T)
  )

tci

### Please note that filter() is the recommended way of splitting the data
 dataex1.s  |>
  summarise(
    Temps = survey_total(JobTmp=="Temporary", vartype = "ci",na.rm=T)
  )


 

```

### Questions

::: panel-tabset
## Questions

1.  Do the frequencies change noticeably when the weight is applied?

2.  Using the code we used to create `JobTmp` above as guide, create a variable to indicate those working part time and examine their weighted and unweighted frequencies. You are going to need this variable later.

## Answers

1.  Yes, the frequencies change quite a lot once we apply the weights — they become much higher. This is because the weights in the Labour Force Survey (LFS) are designed to sum to known UK population totals. That makes it easier to estimate overall population numbers.

    The LFS weights also account for the survey’s sample design: individuals who had a lower chance of being selected are given higher weights to correct for that. They also help adjust for different levels of non-response across subgroups in the population, which means the results are more likely to reflect the population accurately.

2.  The syntax below computes a variable recording whether respondents work part-time or not and produce weighted frequency tables.

```{r pt}

 dataex1 <- dataex1 |> 
             mutate (
               PartTime = case_when(
                  FTPT == 3 | FTPT== 1 ~ "Not part-time",
                  FTPT == 4 | FTPT  == 2 ~ "Part-time",
                  FTPT == -9 | FTPT == -8 ~ NA),
               PartTime = as.factor(PartTime)
                  )


dataex1.s<-dataex1|> 
         as_survey_design(weights=PWT24)


### Unweighted frequencies
table(dataex1$PartTime) 

### Population estimates

svytable(~PartTime, dataex1.s)


t2<-dataex1.s |>
  filter(PartTime=="Part-time") |>
  summarise(
    total = survey_total(vartype = "ci",na.rm=T)
  )

t2


```
:::



## Splitting by working time status and sex

We will now create a table to examine full-time and part-time employees by job tenure.

```{r tmp_ftpt}
t3<-svytable(~PartTime+JobTmp,dataex1.s)

t3 

t4<-dataex1.s |> 
    filter(!is.na(PartTime)) |> 
    group_by(PartTime) |> 
    summarise(
      total = survey_total(
        JobTmp=="Temporary", 
        vartype = "ci",
        na.rm=T)
  )

t4
```

We can  add a third variable to the table to examine the number of temporary and part-time employees by gender.

```{r sex, eval=c(1,2)}
#| echo=c(1,2) 
t5<-svytable(~PartTime+JobTmp+droplevels(as_factor(SEX)),dataex1.s)
t5
```

```{r sexci, eval=c(1,2)}
t6<-dataex1.s |> 
    filter(!is.na(PartTime))|> 
    group_by(SEX,PartTime) |> 
    summarise(survey_total(JobTmp=="Temporary", vartype="ci", na.rm=T))
t6
```

### Review questions

::: panel-tabset
## Questions

1.  How many people are temporary employees (all and part-time) in this quarter?

2.  How many females are in part-time temporary employment?

3.  How can we find out the number of applicable cases for men in part-time temporary employment - ie the number of cases in the sample used to calculate the population counts?

## Answers

There were between `{r} prettyNum(tci$total_low,big.mark = ",")` and `{r} prettyNum(tci$total_upp,big.mark = ",")` temporary employees, of which between `{r} prettyNum(round(t4$total_low[2]),big.mark = ",")` and `{r} prettyNum(round(t4$total_upp[2]),big.mark = ",")` part-time. 

2.  There were between `{r} prettyNum(round(t6[4,4]),big.mark = ",")`  and `{r} prettyNum(round(t6[4,5]),big.mark = ",")` females in part-time temporary employment 

3.  In order to get the number of applicable cases, we need to look at the unweighted frequencies of `SEX` by `JobTmp` by `PartTime`:  

```{r validcases}

table(dataex1$JobTmp,dataex1$PartTime,dataex1$SEX)
```

The number of (unweighted) valid cases for this analysis is only `{r} prettyNum(xtabs(~JobTmp+PartTime+SEX,dataex1)[4],big.mark = ",")`
:::

Note: You can check if your results match those in the [ONS EMP07 dataset](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/employmentandemployeetypes/datasets/temporaryemployeesemp07).
